idiom_name: asyncio.start_server / open_connection with StreamReader and StreamWriter
implementation_notes: The asyncio event loop is the completion dispatcher: it polls the platform (SelectorEventLoop on Unix; ProactorEventLoop, an I/O completion port proactor, is the Windows default since 3.8) and resumes the tasks whose operations completed. The Streams API hides transports and protocols - start_server invokes a per-connection coroutine, open_connection returns a reader/writer pair, and await on read or write suspends until the corresponding completion - while the underlying callback structure stays visible in the transport and protocol layer.
code_sketch:
async def handle(reader, writer):
    data = await reader.read(1024)          # resumes on completion
    writer.write(data)
    await writer.drain()

async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 8080)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()
pitfalls: Anything blocking inside a coroutine (time.sleep, a synchronous driver) freezes the loop; blocking calls belong in asyncio.to_thread or a plain executor.
ProactorEventLoop is Windows-only and supports neither add_reader/add_writer nor pipe connections to non-overlapped handles, so code that works on the selector loop can break on the proactor loop.
Streams must be closed explicitly (writer.close() plus await writer.wait_closed()); abandoned transports leak descriptors.
Task exceptions are swallowed unless the task is awaited or a done callback retrieves them, and cancelling the awaiting coroutine does not interrupt a to_thread worker.

variants.name: Executors with Future completion callbacks
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's threaded asynchronous operation engine, written directly: a ThreadPoolExecutor or ProcessPoolExecutor runs blocking operations, the Future is the completion handle and add_done_callback is the completion dispatcher. It needs no event loop and is the pragmatic choice when the available libraries are blocking; the price is threads, context switches and per-operation state that crosses thread boundaries.
variants.code_sketch:
pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)

def on_accept(fut):                          # completion handler
    conn = fut.result()
    conn.sendall(b"ok")
    pool.submit(accept_one).add_done_callback(on_accept)   # reissue

pool.submit(accept_one).add_done_callback(on_accept)
pitfalls: Callbacks run on the worker thread that completed the operation, so shared state needs synchronization - unlike asyncio, where handlers are single-threaded.
Exceptions stay inside the Future until result() is called; a callback that does not retrieve or log the result hides failures.
A worker that waits on another Future of the same pool can deadlock, as the concurrent.futures documentation warns.
